newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico teachers take to streets, vow to fight on.
newsitem.headline: Mexico teachers take to streets, vow to fight on.

text.p: Thousands of teachers from six states across Mexico held marches in Mexico City on Tuesday to demand pay rises and denounce the jailing and disappearance of 100 of their colleagues.
Several thousand disgruntled teachers blocked the entrance to the Mexican Stock Exchange for nearly an hour and also clogged key avenues in different parts of the city, snarling traffic.
"We have a nationwide list of demands, including a 100-percent pay increase and 90 days of Christmas bonus," Gilberto Nava, a spokesman for marching teachers from the state of Guerrero, told Reuters.
The protesters belong to a dissident teachers union that opposes the officially sanctioned National Education Workers' Union (SNTE), one of the largest unions in Latin America.

The government negotiated a 6 percent payraise and an additional 10 percent in bonuses last week with the SNTE, but the dissident National Education Workers' Coordingating (CNTE) group said the offer fell short.

Public teachers in Mexico earn between 600 pesos ($75) and 1,400 pesos ($177) per month, Nava said. Teachers say their wages have fallen short of inflation, which in the last year was about 22 percent.

The dissident union also claims more than 100 teachers had "disappeared" in the southern states of Michoacan, Guerrero and Oaxaca, in addition to others murdered by state security forces in response to a nationwide teachers strike.

CNTE representatives and the Education Ministry (SEP) had reached agreement on social matters but not on wages, in negotiations that began after 30,000 teachers marched in Mexico City on May 21, Nava said.

CNTE leaders said dissident teachers would continue with a new round of protests, including a march of 100,000 people planned for Wednesday. The protest will be another attempt to reach the President's official Los Pinos residence, he said.
Education Minister Miguel Limon said the ministry was looking into the teachers requests, but added "there can be no increases above those fixed by national negotiations which ended on May 14."
